issues.legal_issue: A pre-emptor who does not exercise the right of pre-emption when it first arises on a transfer cannot claim that right against a later transfer of the same property.
material_facts: The property had been transferred in earlier transactions, including a transfer made after the relevant pre-emption law came into force.
The plaintiff did not challenge the post-commencement transfer.
The plaintiff later sued to enforce pre-emption rights in relation to a subsequent transfer of the same property; the plaintiff’s eligibility to claim pre-emption was otherwise undisputed.
The High Court held the later suit timely, while the trial court and first appellate court had held it barred.
issues.conclusion: The right of pre-emption was exercisable only on the first occasion when it arose. By not exercising it against the earlier post-commencement transfer, the plaintiff waived the right and could not enforce it against the later transfer. The suit was barred, the High Court’s order was set aside, and the trial court and first appellate court orders were upheld.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 3, 6, 8, 9 and 21 of the Rajasthan Pre-Emption Act, 1966, read with Article 97 of the Limitation Act, 1963, govern the right, its exercise and limitation. A pre-emption right is a weak, secondary right of substitution, not a right to the property itself, and must be superior to the vendee’s right when exercised. Under Section 9, failure to exercise the right in relation to a transaction results in its loss; that loss is attributable both to the transaction and to the pre-emptor, so the right does not arise again for that person on a later sale of the same property. The Court relied on Barasat Eye Hospital v. Kaustabh Mondal and Bishan Singh v. Khazan Singh for the nature of the right as substitution; on Indira Bai v. Nand Kishore for the principle that a pre-emptor may give up the right and that it does not pass to anyone; and on the consistent approach in Ghanshyam v. Chand Bihari, Rukmani Devi v. Prabhu Narayan and Prahlad Kumar v. Kishan Chand. The Court distinguished Kutina Bibi v. Baikuntha Chandra Dutta on its facts.

rule.if: preemption_enforcement_suit and earlier_qualifying_transfer and earlier_transfer_not_challenged and later_transfer_of_same_property

predicates.preemption_enforcement_suit: A plaintiff brings a suit seeking to enforce a right of pre-emption.
predicates.earlier_qualifying_transfer: The same property was transferred earlier after the pre-emption right had become legally available to the plaintiff.
predicates.earlier_transfer_not_challenged: The plaintiff did not seek to enforce the pre-emption right in relation to that earlier transfer.
predicates.later_transfer_of_same_property: A later transfer of the same property is the transaction against which the plaintiff seeks pre-emption.
predicates.subsequent_preemption_claim_barred: The plaintiff cannot enforce the pre-emption right against the later transfer.

issues.definition: When a plaintiff sues to enforce pre-emption against a later transfer of property after leaving an earlier qualifying transfer of that same property unchallenged, the claim against the later transfer is barred.
